subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: In Class 10B of a Bengaluru school, the teacher asked who could explain photosynthesis. Jomon's hand went up first. He explained it perfectly, with a few Malayalam-flavoured vowels, and someone near the window said, "Say it in English, bro." Laughter. Then Rhea gave the same answer in a polished accent, and Mrs. Iyer said, "Excellent, very well spoken." Seema watched Jomon's ears go pink. She thought of her own mother, who read Kannada novels faster than anyone Seema knew but went silent at parent meetings. At lunch Seema sat beside Jomon. "Your answer had the chlorophyll part. Hers didn't." He looked up. "Really?" "Really. I checked the book." That evening Seema caught herself mocking a vegetable seller's English on the phone to a friend, and stopped mid-sentence.

qa.q: Which part did Seema say Jomon's answer had and Rhea's did not?
qa.a: Seema said Jomon's answer had the chlorophyll part.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling as she watched Jomon's ears go pink?
qa.a: Seema felt uneasy and sympathetic, recognising the same unfairness her mother faces at parent meetings.

qa.q: What could Mrs. Iyer have done differently?
qa.a: She could have praised Jomon's correct content first and stopped the "say it in English" laughter, showing that an accent says nothing about intelligence.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when the class laughed?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and hurt that a correct answer was mocked just for his vowels, which is why his ears went pink.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager noticing that polished English earns praise while a regional accent is mocked, and resisting that bias in others and in herself.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: At the Pune college fest, the banner committee met in the canteen. "Why is the main board only in Hindi and English?" Vishal demanded. "This is Maharashtra. Marathi goes on top." Hemant, who had come from Patna in first year, shrugged. "Put all three?" "You people always..." Vishal stopped. Hemant's face had closed. The table went quiet. Vishal looked down at his notebook, full of the Marathi poems he wrote at night. "Sorry. That came out wrong. I want our language on the board. Not less of yours." Hemant rubbed his neck and nodded slowly. "Then teach me to write Swagat properly. I'll paint it." That evening the banner said Swagat in large orange Marathi letters, and under it, smaller, the same welcome in Hindi and English, in Hemant's careful brushwork.

qa.q: Where had Hemant come from in first year?
qa.a: Hemant had come from Patna.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he demanded Marathi on top?
qa.a: Vishal felt proud of Marathi and resentful that it was left off, which made him bristle and nearly insult Hemant.

qa.q: What turned the argument around?
qa.a: Vishal noticed Hemant's face close, apologised, and separated love for Marathi from contempt for Hindi, which let Hemant join in.

qa.q: What might Hemant have felt when Vishal said "You people always"?
qa.a: Hemant probably felt hurt and shut out, as if lumped in with a whole group, which is why his face closed.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult's strong pride in his state's language, the pull toward contempt for another, and a friendship that crosses that line.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: So, you want to know what my first month in Chennai was like. Honestly? I'm Kamal, I grew up in Lucknow, and I felt like a parcel with the wrong address. At the vegetable shop I pointed at things like a toddler. The auntie there would say the price in Tamil, fast, and I'd just hold out a note and hope. In class the professor switched to Tamil for jokes and everyone laughed except me. I started eating alone. Then Vandana, who sat next to me in the lab, saw me staring at a menu card. She said "konjam, konjam" means "a little, a little" and made me repeat it. Now I say "Vanakkam, konjam Tamil theriyum" at every shop. The auntie laughs, but she slows down for me. Last week she even threw in an extra drumstick.

qa.q: What phrase does Kamal now say at every shop?
qa.a: Kamal says "Vanakkam, konjam Tamil theriyum" at every shop.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel in the first month, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kamal felt lost and like an outsider, comparing it to being a parcel with the wrong address and starting to eat alone.

qa.q: What small step helped Kamal most?
qa.a: Learning a few basic phrases and using them even with mistakes, which won goodwill and made the shopkeeper slow down.

qa.q: How might the vegetable-shop auntie see Kamal now?
qa.a: She seems amused and warm, slowing down and even adding a drumstick, pleased that Kamal is trying.

grounding: It illustrates a student in a new state struggling at shops and in class, and how learning basic phrases and a local who slows down win goodwill.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
"...so we'll share the revised timeline by Thursday, end of day. Thank you, Martin." Lalit clicked off the call.
His phone buzzed. "Haan, Maa. Khana kha liya. Arre, tension mat lo, chhata le ke gaya tha."
Asif looked up from the next desk, grinning. "Two different people in one minute."
"Same person, two tools," Lalit said. "Martin needs the tidy English. Maa needs me."
"Doesn't it feel fake? I feel fake in meetings sometimes."
"I used to. Then I noticed I don't feel fake speaking Hindi to my Nani and Marwari to my Dadi. Why should English be different?"
"Marwari too?"
"Only with Dadi. If I stop, it goes out of our house."
Asif leaned back. "My Ammi keeps telling me to speak Urdu with my niece."
"Then do it," Lalit said, already typing the timeline email.

qa.q: By when did Lalit promise the revised timeline?
qa.a: By Thursday, end of day.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel about switching between English and home languages?
qa.a: Lalit feels comfortable and whole, not fake, seeing each language as a tool for a different person.

qa.q: What could Asif take from Lalit's approach?
qa.a: Asif could treat meeting English as one tool rather than a mask, and keep Urdu alive by speaking it with the niece as Ammi suggests.

qa.q: Why might Asif feel fake in meetings when Lalit does not?
qa.a: Asif may still see polished English as a different self rather than a register, so switching feels like hiding instead of choosing a tool.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who moves between polished work English and home languages without feeling fake, and keeps a family language alive.

subtype: Village child in a city school [Receiver]
passage: Aiko's first week at the big school in Osaka felt like running after a train. In her mountain village there had been eleven children in one classroom; here there were thirty-four, and they all seemed to know where the shoe lockers were without looking. Her words came out slow and countryish, and when she used her village word for "I", two boys snorted. At lunch she ate facing the wall. On Thursday Mr. Tanaka, the class teacher, asked Javier to show her the recycling rules, which had five different bins. Javier had moved from Valencia only last year. "I put glass in paper for a month," he told her. "Everyone laughs at first. Then they forget." On Friday Mr. Tanaka asked Aiko to tell the class how to plant rice. She knew every step.

qa.q: How many children were in Aiko's village classroom?
qa.a: There were eleven children in one classroom.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when she ate lunch facing the wall?
qa.a: Aiko felt embarrassed and behind, wanting to hide after the boys snorted at her village word.

qa.q: How did Mr. Tanaka help Aiko move from shame toward confidence?
qa.a: He paired her with a friendly classmate for the new rules and then let her teach something she knew well, planting rice.

qa.q: Why might Javier understand Aiko better than the other children?
qa.a: Javier had also moved recently and made mistakes like putting glass in paper, so he knows how embarrassing the first weeks feel and that it passes.

grounding: It illustrates a village child in a city school who feels behind, and how patient teaching and a classmate to sit with begin to turn shame into confidence.

passage:
Hafsa's holiday diary, Day 3.
Best day EVER. Rajni took me to the mango orchard and we ate three each, juice running to our elbows. I stepped in mud up to my ankle and lost a slipper, and Rajni laughed so hard she sat down. The buffalo is called Rani. She breathes like a pressure cooker.
Everything here is slow. Nobody is in a hurry. I told Nani I want to live here forever.
One thing was strange. Rajni had to get up before it was light to carry water from the handpump, and she couldn't come to the pond after lunch because she had to cut fodder. She said, "You're lucky, you're a guest." I didn't know what to say.
Tomorrow we are making mango pickle. I will ask if I can carry water too.

qa.q: What is the buffalo called?
qa.a: The buffalo is called Rani.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling in the orchard, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hafsa felt thrilled and carefree, calling it the best day ever and eating mangoes with juice running to the elbows.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do to understand village life better?
qa.a: Hafsa could ask Rajni about her mornings and actually help with the water, as planned, to see the work behind the slow, sunny days.

qa.q: How might Rajni see Hafsa's holiday?
qa.a: Rajni may feel a little tired or envious, since Hafsa gets to play while she carries water and cuts fodder, which shows in "You're lucky, you're a guest."

grounding: It illustrates a city child thrilled by mud, mangoes and a slower rhythm in a village, with first hints of the hard work behind it.

passage: In a village outside Hue, Mei did her physics problems by a battery lamp after the pigs were fed. She wanted to build bridges, real ones, in the city. The nearest extra classes were in town, an hour away by motorbike, and cost more than her family could spare. When her father hurt his back in the paddy, Mei missed two weeks of school to plant seedlings. She cried once, into the rice, then went back to her equations at night. At the Tet holidays, Mina came home. Mina had grown up two houses away and now worked for a road company in Da Nang. She sat with Mei on the step, looked through the notebook, and said, "Your working is neat. I'll send you my old textbooks, and we'll talk every Sunday on the phone."

qa.q: What did Mei do her physics problems by?
qa.a: She did them by a battery lamp after the pigs were fed.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling when she missed school to plant seedlings?
qa.a: Mei felt sad and frustrated, crying once into the rice, but stayed determined enough to return to the equations at night.

qa.q: Why does Mina's offer matter so much?
qa.a: Mina offers what the village lacks, old textbooks and weekly guidance, which helps fill the gap left by the costly classes in town.

qa.q: What might Mina see when looking through Mei's notebook?
qa.a: Mina probably sees real promise, and perhaps her own younger self, in the neat working, which is why she offers books and Sunday calls.

grounding: It illustrates a rural teenager studying by lamp for a city engineering dream, slowed by cost and family need, and helped by a local mentor.

passage: Six-fifteen alarm, six-fifty bus, and the bus takes forty minutes in Gurugram traffic if we're lucky. That's my morning. I'm Parul, Class 11, and people tell me I'm lucky to live in a city with everything, and I am: three libraries, a coding club, the best tuition teachers. But after school it's tuition till eight, then homework, then I scroll and see everyone's trips and toppers' lists and feel I'm already behind at sixteen. There's no ground near our society, just a parking lot. Last month my friend Vaibhav made me walk with him around the lot after dinner, twenty minutes, no phones. It sounds so silly. But it's the only part of my day nobody grades. I sleep better on the days we walk.

qa.q: Where do Parul and Vaibhav walk after dinner?
qa.a: They walk around the parking lot after dinner.

qa.q: What does Parul feel when scrolling after homework?
qa.a: Parul feels anxious and behind, comparing a crowded day with everyone's trips and toppers' lists.

qa.q: What small balance in Parul's day seems to help, and why?
qa.a: The twenty-minute walk with no phones gives a space nobody grades, easing the stress and helping sleep.

qa.q: Why might Vaibhav have insisted on the walks?
qa.a: Vaibhav probably noticed Parul looking stressed or lonely and cared enough to start a small, calm routine they could share.

grounding: It illustrates a city teenager with real gains in choice and speed but crowded days, tuition and online comparison, and a small balance that eases stress.

subtype: Looked down on as gaon wala [Receiver]
passage:
"Arre Ganga, is that your Nani's kurta?" Rohan called across the corridor. "Say it for us, say 'ishkool'!"
Laughter. Ganga's grip tightened on her file.
"Leave it, Rohan," Bhupen said, stepping beside her. "She topped the statistics quiz. You came ninth."
"I'm just joking, yaar."
"Then laugh at yourself."
Rohan wandered off. Ganga let out a breath. "I hate that word. Gaon-wali. As if it means dirt."
"Is it true you can tell rain's coming from the sky?" Bhupen asked.
"From the ants, mostly." She almost smiled. "Baba taught me."
"Teach me. And sit with us in the library at four. Priya wants help with the regression problems."
"Only if nobody asks me to say school again."
"Deal."

qa.q: What position did Rohan come in the statistics quiz?
qa.a: Rohan came ninth.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when Rohan mocked her kurta and accent?
qa.a: Ganga felt hurt and humiliated, gripping her file hard and later saying she hates being called gaon-wali "as if it means dirt".

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that other classmates could copy?
qa.a: Bhupen stood beside Ganga, answered the mockery calmly, then showed real interest in what she knows and invited her to study with the group.

qa.q: How might Rohan's joke look to the others in the corridor after Bhupen spoke?
qa.a: Once Bhupen pointed to the quiz results, the joke probably looked petty rather than funny, and the laughter lost its target.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult from a village mocked in a city college for dress and accent, where pride in roots and an including peer show more class than the teasing.

passage: I'm Minakshi, and I'll admit I had decided about Kunal before his bus even reached our village. City boys, I thought, love only their phones and forget their grandparents. For two days he did sit on the charpai with earphones in while we cut the sugarcane. I said something sharp to Amma about it. On the third morning our Dadaji's breathing went bad. Kunal was the one who already knew which hospital in town had the right machine, phoned ahead, and sat with Dadaji in the jeep, holding the oxygen mask steady. Later I learnt he had been on calls with his office all those two days, arguing for leave they did not want to give. I still can't say what he feels about our village. But I don't think selfish is the word.

qa.q: What were the others doing while Kunal sat on the charpai?
qa.a: They were cutting the sugarcane.

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel toward Kunal during the first two days?
qa.a: Minakshi felt irritated and judgemental, already sure that city boys love only their phones.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do the next time a city visitor arrives?
qa.a: Minakshi could wait, or simply ask what someone is busy with, before deciding, since Kunal's calls turned out to be about getting leave, not selfishness.

qa.q: How might Kunal have experienced those first two days in the village?
qa.a: Kunal was probably stressed, caught between office calls and a family visit, and may have felt the family's cool judgement without a chance to explain.

grounding: It illustrates a young villager who sees a city visitor as selfish and cut off from family, then finds the stereotype partly unfair.
